about: The editable standard examples and the failure examples, as model records of schema version 1 (src/record.js). Each variable, equation, condition and assumption has a stable id. Values are illustrative inputs for the example, not measured data.

examples.label: Convection: Pi groups
examples.title: Convective heat transfer: the worked Buckingham Pi calculation

purpose.question: On which independent dimensionless groups does the heat-transfer coefficient of a body in a flow depend?

geometry.domain: A body of characteristic length L in a uniform flow of speed U
geometry.coordinates: None, because the calculation uses the Pi variables only

assumptions.text: All reference quantities are positive.
The inputs have no additional constraints.
k is the conductivity of the fluid, so hL/k is a Nusselt number and not a Biot number.

evidence.claim: The worked calculation gives rank 4 and the groups hL/k, μ/(ρUL) and ρc_pUL/k for the repeating variables ρ, U, L, k.

examples.label: Straight fin
examples.title: Straight fin with an insulated tip: the complete Pi basis

purpose.question: On which dimensionless groups does the base heat flow of a fin with a constant cross-section and an insulated tip depend?

variables.meaning: Heat flow at the fin base

geometry.domain: A straight fin of length L, constant cross-section A_c and exposed perimeter P
geometry.coordinates: x along the fin, from the base (x = 0) to the tip (x = L)
geometry.interfaces: The base at x = 0 and the insulated tip at x = L

assumptions.text: The conductivity is constant.
The surface convection is uniform.
The tip is insulated.
ΔT = T_b − T_∞ is not 0.
Temperature varies along x only. The transverse-conduction validity condition needs a separate derivation.

evidence.claim: The time row equals −3 times the mass row, the rank is 3 and the variable set has 4 independent groups.
m²L² = hPL²/(kA) is the fin parameter of the insulated-tip solution.

examples.label: Transient slab
examples.title: Transient slab with surface convection: the groups before nondimensionalization

purpose.question: On which dimensionless groups does the temperature depend in a slab that cools by convection at its surface?

variables.meaning: Local excess of temperature, T − T_∞
Initial excess of temperature, T_i − T_∞

geometry.domain: A slab of half-thickness L, symmetric about its centre plane
geometry.coordinates: x from the centre plane (x = 0) to the surface (x = L), and time t
geometry.interfaces: The surface at x = L, in contact with a fluid at T_∞

assumptions.text: The material properties are constant.
The slab is symmetric about its centre plane.
T_i is not equal to T_∞.
ρ and c_p enter the equation only as ρc_p, so α = k/(ρc_p) replaces them in the Pi set.

evidence.claim: The slab conditions and the groups X, Fo = τ, θ and Bi.
The separation-of-variables solution of the plane wall with convection and a symmetry condition at the centre line.

examples.label: Lumped body
examples.title: Lumped body cooled by convection: the dimensionless decay

purpose.question: Which dimensionless variables describe the cooling of a small body whose temperature stays uniform?

variables.meaning: Initial excess of temperature, T_i − T_∞

geometry.domain: A small steel cube with a side of 1 cm, cooled by a fluid on all six faces
geometry.coordinates: Time t only: the lumped model has no spatial coordinate
geometry.interfaces: The surface A_s, in contact with a fluid at T_∞

assumptions.text: The temperature is uniform in the body. This needs a small Biot number hL_c/k with L_c = V/A_s. The regime map compares the lumped model with the spatial model of the cube.
The properties and h are constant.
T_i is not equal to T_∞.
ρ and c_p enter the equation only as ρc_p, and V and A_s only as V/A_s. So C = ρc_p and L_c = V/A_s replace them in the Pi set.

evidence.claim: The lumped body with convection: Bi, the dimensionless time and the temperature ratio.

examples.label: Transient cylinder
examples.title: Transient long cylinder with surface convection: the radial modes and the regime map

purpose.question: When is the temperature of a long cylinder that cools by convection close to uniform, and which simple model is accurate at each time?

variables.meaning: Local excess of temperature, T − T_∞
Initial excess of temperature, T_i − T_∞
Thermal conductivity of the long cylinder

geometry.domain: A steel rod of radius R = 25 mm and length H = 0.5 m, cooled in an air blast
geometry.coordinates: r from the centre (r = 0) to the surface (r = R), and time t
geometry.interfaces: The surface at r = R, in contact with a fluid at T_∞

assumptions.text: The material properties are constant.
Heat flows in r only: H/R = 20, so the ends have a small effect. The model neglects them.
T_i is not equal to T_∞.
ρ and c_p enter the equation only as ρc_p, so α = k/(ρc_p) replaces them in the Pi set.

scales.reason: The radius is the length scale, so X = r/R runs from 0 at the centre to 1 at the surface.

evidence.claim: The transient cylinder: radius-based Bi and Fo, and geometry ratios.

examples.label: Transient sphere
examples.title: Transient sphere with surface convection: the radial modes and the regime map

purpose.question: When is the temperature of a sphere that cools by convection close to uniform, and which simple model is accurate at each time?

variables.meaning: Local excess of temperature, T − T_∞
Initial excess of temperature, T_i − T_∞

geometry.domain: A steel ball of radius R = 1 cm, quenched in water
geometry.coordinates: r from the centre (r = 0) to the surface (r = R), and time t
geometry.interfaces: The surface at r = R, in contact with a fluid at T_∞

assumptions.text: The material properties are constant.
Heat flows in r only: the surface condition is the same at every point.
T_i is not equal to T_∞.
ρ and c_p enter the equation only as ρc_p, so α = k/(ρc_p) replaces them in the Pi set.

scales.reason: The radius is the length scale, so X = r/R runs from 0 at the centre to 1 at the surface.

evidence.claim: The transient sphere: radius-based Bi and Fo.

examples.label: Volumetric source
examples.title: Slab with a uniform heat source: the steady temperature and its regimes

purpose.question: Does an electrically heated plate stay inside its allowed temperature rise, and which simple model is accurate?

variables.meaning: Local excess of temperature, T − T_∞
Allowed temperature rise above the fluid

geometry.domain: A plate of half-thickness L = 10 mm with a uniform electric heat source, cooled on both faces
geometry.coordinates: x from the centre plane (x = 0) to the surface (x = L)
geometry.interfaces: The surfaces at x = ±L, in contact with a fluid at T_∞

assumptions.text: The source, the conductivity and h are constant.
The plate is at steady state.
ΔT_ref = 50 K is the allowed rise of the plate temperature above the fluid. It is a positive reference scale.

scales.reason: The allowed rise is the temperature scale, so θ ≤ 1 means that the plate stays inside the allowance.

evidence.claim: The solid with volumetric heat generation: q'''L²/(kΔT) and the boundary parameters.

examples.label: Multilayer wall
examples.title: Two-layer wall with a contact resistance: heat flux, temperature jump and regimes

purpose.question: How much does the contact resistance between an aluminium plate and a steel wall reduce the heat flow?

variables.meaning: Difference of the fluid temperatures, T_∞1 − T_∞2

geometry.domain: An aluminium plate (layer 1, 10 mm) pressed on a steel wall (layer 2, 10 mm), with a hot fluid at face 1 and a cool fluid at face 2
geometry.coordinates: x from face 1 (x = 0) through the contact (x = L_1) to face 2 (x = L_1 + L_2)
geometry.interfaces: The contact between the layers at x = L_1, with the resistance R''_c

assumptions.text: Steady state, with constant properties in each layer.
Heat flows in x only.
The contact resistance R''_c is a measured input per unit area, not a mechanical contact model.
T_∞1 is not equal to T_∞2.

scales.reason: The thickness of layer 1 is the length scale of both layers.
Both layers share the offset T_∞2 and the scale T_∞1 − T_∞2, so θ = 1 at fluid 1 and θ = 0 at fluid 2.
Both layers share the offset T_∞2 and the scale T_∞1 − T_∞2, so θ = 1 at fluid 1 and θ = 0 at fluid 2.

evidence.claim: The multilayer wall: conductivity ratios, thickness ratios and the normalized contact resistance.
